→
Business expectations drive SLA targets. SLAs drive OLA requirements. OLAs drive supplier
commitments. Supplier commitments enable service performance. Misalignment at any point breaks
the chain.
And:
An SLA is not simply a number. It is an agreement about expected service outcomes.
F6.13 — Suppliers, Managed Services & Operational Partners
No enterprise operates technology alone. Suppliers, providers, and partners are integral to service
delivery. Governing them is integral to operations.
Managed service providers deliver operational services on behalf of the enterprise: infrastructure
management, application support, security operations, or service desk. They extend enterprise
capability but do not replace enterprise accountability.
Outsourcing transfers specific functions to external providers: development, operations, support, or
infrastructure. Outsourcing reduces direct control but can improve scale, expertise, and cost efficiency.
Accountability remains with the enterprise.
Cloud providers deliver infrastructure, platform, and software services. Their operational

performance directly affects enterprise service quality. Cloud governance is operational governance.
SaaS providers deliver application services. Their availability, performance, and security are
enterprise concerns. SaaS management requires vendor oversight, integration governance, and data
protection.
Support contracts define the operational relationship with vendors: response times, resolution
commitments, escalation paths, and service credits. They must be monitored and enforced.
Supplier governance ensures that external providers deliver as committed: performance review,
contract compliance, risk monitoring, and relationship management. Governance is not adversarial. It
is the discipline of ensuring partnership delivers value.
Operational Level Agreements define internal commitments between teams that support end-to-end
service delivery. They must align with and support external SLAs.
Underpinning contracts are the agreements with suppliers that enable service delivery. They must be
visible, aligned, and governed.
114

Vendor escalation is the mechanism for addressing supplier underperformance: operational
escalation, commercial escalation, and contractual action. Escalation paths must be defined before they
are needed.
Supplier performance must be measured continuously: availability, responsiveness, quality, and
value. Performance data enables objective conversation and informed decisions.
Multi-vendor environments require coordination: multiple suppliers delivering interdependent
services. Without coordination, gaps emerge, conflicts occur, and accountability fragments.
Service Integration and Management (SIAM) is the discipline of integrating multiple suppliers into a
coherent service delivery ecosystem. SIAM provides governance, coordination, and end-to-end
accountability across vendor boundaries.
Shared service outcomes require coordinated responsibilities across enterprise teams and suppliers.
Contracts and operating models should make responsibilities explicit, while end-to-end accountability
for the service remains clear within the enterprise.
End-to-end service ownership means that someone in the enterprise is accountable for service quality
regardless of how many suppliers contribute. Ownership cannot be outsourced.
Vendor dependency is the risk that the enterprise relies too heavily on a single supplier for critical
capability. Dependency reduces leverage, increases cost, and constrains flexibility.
Service reviews are the periodic assessments of supplier performance: what worked, what failed, what
improved, what needs attention. Reviews must be honest, documented, and action-oriented.
Supplier improvement plans address persistent underperformance: specific deficiencies,
improvement targets, timelines, resources, and verification. Plans must be tracked and enforced.

At Foundation level, SIAM belongs here because F5 addresses commercial delivery and vendor
selection, while F6 addresses ongoing operational supplier performance, coordination, and end-to-end
service integration.
F6.14 — Operational Metrics, KPIs & Service Reporting
Measurement is the discipline of knowing whether operations are healthy. Without measurement,
operations drifts. With poor measurement, operations optimizes the wrong things.
Service availability is the proportion of time services are operational. It is the most visible operational
metric.
SLA achievement measures whether services meet their agreed targets: availability, response time,
resolution time, and performance. Achievement confirms commitment. Breach signals problem.
Incident volume tracks the number of disruptions: total incidents, by service, by category, by severity,
by trend. Volume reveals stability or fragility.
Major incidents count the disruptions that caused significant business impact. Frequency of major
incidents is a critical health indicator.
Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) measures how quickly problems are identified: from occurrence to
awareness. Rapid detection reduces impact.
Mean Time to Acknowledge (MTTA) measures how quickly incidents are recognised and response
initiated: from detection to assignment. Rapid acknowledgment accelerates recovery.
115

Mean Time to Restore / Recover (MTTR) measures how quickly service is restored: from detection to
recovery. Rapid restoration minimizes business impact.
First Contact Resolution measures the proportion of issues resolved at first support interaction. It
indicates support effectiveness and knowledge quality.
Resolution time measures how long incidents take to fix: from logging to closure. It reflects support
capability, complexity, and process efficiency.
Reopened tickets measure incidents that were closed prematurely or incompletely: returned by users,
recurring symptoms, or unresolved root causes. Reopened tickets signal quality failure.
Backlog measures unresolved work: incidents, problems, changes, requests. Growing backlog indicates
capacity constraint, process failure, or demand surge.
Change success rate measures the proportion of changes that achieve their intent without causing
incidents. It reflects change discipline and operational maturity.
Failed change rate measures changes that caused incidents or required rollback. It signals process
weakness or risk underestimation.
Problem recurrence measures whether problems are truly fixed or merely suppressed. Recurrence
indicates ineffective root cause analysis or incomplete corrective action.
Capacity utilisation measures how intensively resources are used: CPU, memory, storage, network. It
enables optimisation and investment planning.
Customer satisfaction measures user perception of service quality: responsiveness, effectiveness,
communication, and empathy. Satisfaction is subjective but essential.
Service experience extends beyond satisfaction to measure effort, emotion, and outcome: how easy
was it, how did it feel, did it work?

Cost per service / ticket measures operational efficiency: total cost divided by volume. It enables
comparison, benchmarking, and optimisation. But cost reduction must not degrade quality.
Trend analysis examines metrics over time: improving, degrading, stable, cyclical, or anomalous.
Trends reveal patterns that single points miss.
Executive dashboards provide concise, visual, real-time operational health: status, trends, alerts, and
key metrics. Dashboards must highlight what matters for decision-making.
Leading vs. lagging indicators is the measurement discipline. Lagging indicators confirm results:
availability achieved, incidents resolved, costs incurred. Leading indicators predict results: monitoring
coverage, change backlog, training completion, knowledge freshness. Effective measurement tracks
both.
But emphasize:
Metrics should support decisions, not merely produce reports.
The organisation that measures everything and decides nothing is not data-driven. It is data-drowned.
The discipline is in selecting the metrics that matter, interpreting them with judgment, and acting on
them with speed.
116

Part VI — Sustain & Improve
F6.15 — Knowledge Management & Operational Documentation
A service that depends on what one person remembers is not operationally mature. Knowledge must be
captured, shared, maintained, and applied.
Knowledge management is the discipline of creating, organizing, sharing, and maintaining the
information that enables operations: procedures, solutions, workarounds, insights, and lessons.
Knowledge articles are the documented solutions to known issues: symptoms, causes, resolutions, and
verification. They enable rapid incident response and self-service.
Known errors are the documented problems with identified root causes and available workarounds.
They accelerate incident response while permanent fixes are developed.
Runbooks are the step-by-step procedures for operational tasks: system startup, failover execution,
backup verification, incident response. They are the operational memory that enables consistent
execution.
SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures) define routine activities: provisioning, patching, access
management, change implementation. They ensure consistency, compliance, and quality.
Technical documentation captures system design, configuration, architecture, and interfaces. It
enables understanding, maintenance, and evolution.
Support documentation captures service information: what the service does, who uses it, how to
access it, how to get help, and what to expect. It empowers users and reduces support burden.
Service documentation combines business and technical information: service description, owner,
dependencies, SLAs, contacts, and procedures. It is the single source of service truth.
Knowledge ownership is the accountability for maintaining specific knowledge: accuracy, currency,

completeness, and accessibility. Knowledge without ownership decays.
Knowledge transfer ensures that expertise moves from individuals to the organisation:
documentation, training, mentoring, and shadowing. Transfer prevents loss when people leave.
Knowledge retention preserves organisational memory: capturing expertise before departure,
documenting decisions, and maintaining historical context.
Shift handover transfers operational context between teams: what happened, what is happening, what
needs attention, what is scheduled. Poor handover creates gaps and errors.
Vendor knowledge transfer ensures that external expertise becomes internal capability: training,
documentation, shadowing, and practice. Dependency on vendor knowledge creates risk.
Self-service knowledge empowers users to resolve issues independently: searchable articles, guided
procedures, and automated assistance. It reduces cost and accelerates resolution.
Lessons learned capture insights from incidents, changes, projects, and reviews: what worked, what
failed, what should change. They must be documented, shared, and applied.
Knowledge quality measures accuracy, completeness, currency, accessibility, and usefulness. Poor
knowledge is worse than no knowledge because it creates false confidence.
117

AI-assisted knowledge management uses machine learning to suggest solutions, auto-generate
articles, identify gaps, and improve search. It amplifies human effort but requires quality data and clear
governance.
Core principle:
A service that depends on what one person remembers is not operationally mature.
F6.16 — Automation, AIOps & Intelligent Operations
Operations is evolving from manual execution to intelligent adaptation. This section creates an
important connection back to F2 without repeating AI fundamentals.
Operational automation replaces manual tasks with automated execution: provisioning, patching,
backup, monitoring, alerting, and remediation. Automation increases speed, consistency, and scale. It
also amplifies error and requires governance.
Workflow automation orchestrates sequences of operational tasks: incident routing, change approval,
access provisioning, and report generation. It reduces delay and enforces process.
Infrastructure automation manages cloud and on-premises resources as code: provisioning,
configuration, scaling, and retirement. It enables consistency, repeatability, and auditability.
Automated remediation responds to detected issues without human intervention: restart failed
services, reroute traffic, scale resources, or apply workarounds. It accelerates recovery but requires
careful boundary definition.
Self-healing is the advanced form of automated remediation: systems that detect, diagnose, and resolve
issues without human involvement. Self-healing reduces operational burden but requires robust design
and human oversight.
Event correlation connects related operational events into coherent incidents: multiple alerts from the
same root cause, cascading failures, and common-mode problems. Correlation reduces noise and

accelerates diagnosis.
AIOps (Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations) uses machine learning to analyse operational data:
predict failures, correlate events, recommend actions, and automate responses. AIOps amplifies human
capability but requires quality data, clear boundaries, and continuous validation.
Predictive operations anticipates problems before they cause incidents: capacity exhaustion,
performance degradation, failure patterns, and anomaly detection. Prediction enables proactive
intervention.
Anomaly detection identifies behaviour that deviates from baseline: unusual traffic, unexpected
errors, abnormal resource consumption. Anomaly detection reveals emerging problems before
thresholds are breached.
AI-assisted service desk uses natural language processing to understand user requests, suggest
solutions, route issues, and fulfill routine requests. It scales support capacity but requires quality
knowledge and human fallback.
Intelligent routing directs issues to the most appropriate resolver based on content, skill, availability,
and history. It reduces resolution time and improves first-contact resolution.
118

AI knowledge assistants help users find information, answer questions, and resolve issues through
conversational interaction. They require curated knowledge and continuous learning.
Predictive capacity management forecasts demand and optimizes resources: when to scale, when to
invest, when to consolidate. It improves efficiency and reduces waste.
Automation risks include over-automation, brittle scripts, cascading failures, loss of human judgment,
and governance gaps. Automation must be governed as rigorously as manual work.
Human oversight ensures that automated systems operate within defined boundaries: escalation
triggers, exception handling, and intervention protocols. Humans must remain accountable for
automated decisions.
Governance of operational AI defines who decides what AI can do, how its decisions are monitored,
how errors are corrected, and how accountability is maintained.
Progression:
Manual
Standardized
Automated
Predictive
Adaptive
→
→
→
→
Manual work requires human effort for every instance. Standardized work follows defined procedures.
Automated work executes without human intervention. Predictive work anticipates and prevents.
Adaptive work learns and optimizes continuously.
F6.17 — Continual Improvement & Service Maturity
Figure — Service operations and continual improvement
Stable operations are not static operations. The discipline of improvement is what separates mature
operations from declining ones.
119

Continual improvement is the ongoing practice of identifying opportunities, prioritizing actions,
implementing changes, and verifying results. It is not a project. It is a permanent organisational habit.
Improvement opportunities emerge from many sources: incidents, problems, changes, audits,
feedback, benchmarks, and innovation. They must be captured, evaluated, and prioritised.
Improvement register is the inventory of identified opportunities: description, benefit, cost, risk,
priority, owner, and status. It ensures that opportunities are not lost and that improvement is visible.
Baselines establish current performance: availability, cost, satisfaction, efficiency, and quality.
Baselines enable measurement of improvement.
Targets define desired future performance: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound.
Targets provide direction and motivation.
Prioritisation determines which improvements to pursue: impact, feasibility, resource requirement,
strategic alignment, and risk. Not every opportunity should be pursued. The discipline is in choosing
wisely.
Root-cause-driven improvement addresses the fundamental causes of operational pain: recurring
incidents, chronic problems, process failures, and capability gaps. It prevents symptoms rather than
treating them.
Automation opportunities identify where manual effort can be reduced, consistency increased, and
speed accelerated. Automation is a primary lever of operational improvement.
Customer feedback reveals where services fail to meet expectations: complaints, suggestions, surveys,
and behavioural data. Feedback is the voice of the user in improvement.
Service reviews assess service performance, identify improvement areas, and commit to action. They

are the operational dialogue between provider and consumer.
Operational maturity describes the sophistication of operational practices: from ad hoc to defined,
from defined to measured, from measured to managed, from managed to optimised. Maturity is not a
destination. It is a continuous journey.
Process maturity describes the sophistication of specific operational processes: incident management,
change enablement, problem management, service level management. Each process matures
independently and requires individual attention.
Service maturity describes the overall capability of a service: its reliability, efficiency, responsiveness,
and value. Mature services are predictable, cost-effective, and aligned to business need.
Benchmarking compares operational performance against peers, standards, or aspirational targets.
Benchmarking reveals gaps, validates progress, and identifies opportunities.
Lessons learned capture insights from operational experience: what worked, what failed, what should
change. They must be documented, shared, and applied.
Improvement ownership is the accountability for specific improvements: identifying, planning,
implementing, and verifying. Improvements without owners are wishes.
Benefits measurement confirms that improvement achieved its intent: cost reduced, quality increased,
speed accelerated, satisfaction improved. Measurement validates investment and guides future
prioritisation.
Simple model:

Understand

Improve
Verify
Repeat
→
→
→

→
Measurement reveals current state. Understanding identifies causes and opportunities. Prioritisation
focuses effort. Improvement implements change. Verification confirms results. Repetition sustains
discipline.
Core principle:
Stable operations are not static operations.
The enterprise that believes it has achieved operational excellence and stops improving is already
declining. Excellence is not a state. It is a practice.
F6.18 — Executive Operations Case Study
This section brings F6 together through an integrated scenario. Read it as an exercise in applying
everything this chapter has established.
The situation:
A critical enterprise digital service is experiencing recurring outages, slow response times, growing
ticket volumes, failed changes, vendor disputes, poor SLA performance, incomplete monitoring, and
frustrated business users.
The learner must determine:

What is the immediate operational priority? — Which incidents, problems, or risks demand
urgent attention?

Which incidents require major-incident handling? — What criteria trigger major incident
response, and what structure is needed?

What recurring problems require root-cause investigation? — Which patterns indicate
underlying problems that incident management alone cannot solve?

Is monitoring and observability sufficient? — What visibility exists, what is missing, and what
would enable faster detection and diagnosis?

Are operational changes properly controlled? — What is the change success rate, what failures
occurred, and what governance is needed?

Are SLAs and supplier responsibilities appropriate? — Do agreements reflect business need, are
they monitored, and are they enforced?


Which KPIs should executives monitor? — What metrics reveal operational health, and what
decisions do they enable?

What should be automated or improved? — Where does manual effort create risk or delay, and
where would improvement create greatest value?
Then:

What should leadership do now, and why? — What decisions, investments, or interventions are
required, with what rationale and what expected outcome?
The scenario uses structured questions and emphasises reasoning over prescribed answers.

F7 — Cybersecurity, Risk & Resilience
Foundation
Purpose
Build your ability to understand cybersecurity, technology risk, information protection, privacy,
resilience, and continuity as enterprise leadership responsibilities — not merely technical security
functions.
This chapter teaches how organisations identify what matters, understand threats and vulnerabilities,
assess risk, establish proportionate controls, respond to incidents, recover from disruption, and
continuously strengthen resilience.
By the end of F7, you should be able to answer:
"How do we protect the enterprise's technology, information, services, and stakeholders
— while managing risk proportionately and ensuring the organisation can withstand,
respond to, and recover from disruption?"
Part I — Understand Risk & Security
F7.1 — What Are Cybersecurity, Information Security & Technology Risk?
Security is not about eliminating risk. It is about understanding risk and reducing it to an
acceptable level.
This distinction matters. Many organisations pursue security as if risk could be eliminated: more
controls, more tools, more policies, more audits. This pursuit is futile and destructive. It consumes
resources, paralyzes decision-making, and creates the illusion of safety without the reality of protection.
Security is not the absence of risk. It is the disciplined management of risk.
Cybersecurity is the protection of digital environments: networks, systems, applications, data, and
identities from digital threats. It is the technical and operational discipline of defending against cyber
attacks, detecting intrusions, responding to breaches, and recovering from compromise.
Information security is broader. It protects information in all forms — digital, physical, verbal —

throughout its lifecycle: creation, storage, processing, transmission, and destruction. Information
security encompasses cybersecurity but extends to physical documents, verbal communications, and
human behaviour.
123

Technology risk is the possibility that technology failures, vulnerabilities, or compromises will cause
harm to the enterprise: financial loss, operational disruption, reputational damage, regulatory penalty,
or competitive disadvantage. Technology risk is not limited to security. It includes availability, integrity,
performance, and compliance.
Operational risk is the possibility that operational failures — human error, process breakdown, system
failure, or external events — will cause harm. Technology risk is a subset of operational risk, but
technology increasingly permeates every operational domain.
Digital risk is the broader category of risk arising from the enterprise's digital presence and activities:
cyber threats, data breaches, platform failures, digital fraud, online reputation, and regulatory
exposure.
Cyber risk is the specific risk arising from cyber threats: attacks, intrusions, malware, ransomware,
espionage, and sabotage. It is the most visible and visceral form of technology risk.
Security vs. risk is the fundamental relationship. Security is the practice of protection. Risk is the
measure of what is being protected against, at what likelihood, with what impact, and at what cost.
Security without risk understanding is theater. Risk without security response is resignation.
Protection vs. resilience is the strategic balance. Protection prevents harm: controls, defenses,
barriers, and deterrence. Resilience survives harm: recovery, adaptation, continuity, and learning.
Both are essential. Protection reduces frequency. Resilience reduces severity. The enterprise that
protects without resilience will eventually fail. The enterprise that pursues resilience without protection
will fail frequently.

Business impact of cyber risk is not merely technical. A data breach affects customer trust, regulatory
standing, competitive position, and executive accountability. A ransomware attack halts operations,
destroys revenue, and damages reputation. A supply-chain compromise exposes partners, customers,
and markets. Cyber risk is enterprise risk.
Security as a business responsibility means that cybersecurity cannot be delegated entirely to the
CISO, IT, or compliance teams. Governing bodies provide oversight and approve risk direction;
executives own business outcomes and risk decisions within their authority; security leaders provide
specialist leadership; and every employee has defined responsibilities.
Role of IT leadership in security is to ensure that technology risk is understood, governed, and
managed as an enterprise discipline. The CIO or IT Director does not need to be the deepest security
expert. They need to be the leader who ensures that security serves business objectives, that risk is
proportionate to value, and that protection does not paralyze progress.
Shared responsibility means that security responsibilities are distributed across the enterprise.
Business owners, technology teams, security, HR, Legal, Procurement, Risk, suppliers, and users each
have defined responsibilities. Accountability should be explicit rather than assumed.
Risk-based security means that protection is proportionate to risk: more controls where risk is high,
fewer where risk is low, and continuous adjustment as risk evolves. Risk-based security is efficient.
Compliance-based security is often wasteful.
Security governance is the framework of policies, standards, roles, and processes that ensure security

is managed as an enterprise discipline: strategy, risk assessment, control selection, incident response,
assurance, and improvement.
Important distinction:
124

Cybersecurity protects digital environments. Information security protects information in all
forms. Risk management determines what protection is proportionate.
Key principle:
Security is not about eliminating risk. It is about understanding risk and reducing it to an
acceptable level.
F7.2 — Information & Technology Assets
Before protecting anything, the enterprise must know what it is protecting. Invisibility is the enemy of
security.
Information assets are the data and knowledge the enterprise creates, collects, processes, and stores:
customer records, financial data, intellectual property, employee information, operational data,
strategic plans, and communications. Information assets are not merely digital. They include physical
documents, verbal knowledge, and contractual obligations.
Technology assets are the systems, infrastructure, and platforms that process, store, and transmit
information: servers, networks, applications, databases, cloud services, endpoints, and mobile devices.
Applications are the software systems that process information and enable business processes. Their
security depends on design, configuration, maintenance, and use.
Infrastructure is the foundational technology: servers, storage, networks, data centers, and cloud
platforms. Its security depends on configuration, patching, access control, and monitoring.
Data is often among the enterprise’s most valuable and vulnerable assets. Its security depends on
classification, access control, encryption, lifecycle management, and governance.
Cloud services extend the enterprise's technology footprint beyond its direct control. Their security
depends on shared responsibility, configuration discipline, and vendor governance.

Endpoints are the devices through which users access enterprise resources: laptops, desktops, mobile
phones, tablets, and IoT devices. Their security depends on configuration, protection, monitoring, and
user behaviour.
Networks are the connectivity that links assets, users, and services. Their security depends on
segmentation, access control, encryption, and monitoring.
Identity is the digital representation of users, services, and devices. Its security depends on
authentication, authorization, lifecycle management, and governance.
Third-party services are the external capabilities the enterprise consumes: SaaS, cloud, managed
services, and supplier platforms. Their security depends on contractual requirements, assessment,
monitoring, and incident coordination.
Asset inventory is the complete, accurate, and maintained record of what the enterprise owns,
operates, or accesses. You cannot protect what you do not know exists.
Asset ownership is the accountability for an asset's protection, maintenance, and lifecycle. Every asset
must have a named owner.
Data ownership is the business accountability for data classification, quality, access policy, and
appropriate use. Data owners are typically business leaders, not IT staff.
126

Classification is the categorization of assets by sensitivity and criticality: public, internal, confidential,
restricted. Classification determines protection requirements.
Criticality is the ranking of assets by importance to business operations: critical, important, supporting,
discretionary. Criticality determines resilience investment.
Business impact is the consequence of asset compromise, loss, or unavailability: revenue, operations,
reputation, compliance, and safety.
Asset lifecycle is the journey from acquisition to retirement: procurement, deployment, operation,
maintenance, and disposal. Security must be managed at every stage.
Shadow IT is the technology that operates outside enterprise visibility and governance: unauthorized
cloud services, personal devices, unapproved applications. Shadow IT creates invisible risk.
Unknown assets are the systems, data, and connections that the enterprise does not know it has. They
are unprotected because they are unseen.
Asset dependencies are the relationships where one asset's security depends on another: an
application depends on a database, which depends on infrastructure, which depends on a vendor.
Dependencies determine cascading impact.
Core model:
Identify
Classify
Own
Protect
Monitor
Retire
→
→
→
→
→
Assets should be identified, classified, assigned accountable ownership, protected according to risk,
monitored throughout their useful life, and retired securely. This model connects back to F3
architecture and F6 configuration/service management without repeating them.
F7.3 — Security Principles & Protection Objectives
Security language must be precise. Imprecision creates gaps that attackers exploit and that governance
misses.
CIA Triad is the foundational model:


Confidentiality — information is accessible only to authorised parties

Integrity — information is accurate, complete, and unaltered

Availability — information and systems are accessible when needed
These three objectives are necessary but no longer sufficient.
Modern security extends the triad:

Authenticity — the identity of users, systems, and data can be verified

Accountability — actions can be traced to responsible parties

Non-repudiation — actions cannot be denied by those who performed them

Privacy — personal information is collected, used, and protected appropriately

Safety — where applicable, technology does not cause physical harm
Least privilege means that access is granted at the minimum level necessary for the specific task, for
the minimum time required. It is not merely "don't give admin rights." It is a continuous discipline of
access minimization.
Need-to-know means that information is accessible only to those whose role requires it. It is the
information equivalent of least privilege.
127

Separation of duties means that critical functions are divided among multiple people to prevent fraud,
error, and abuse. No single person should control an entire sensitive process.
Defense in depth means that security is layered: multiple controls at multiple levels so that the failure
of one does not compromise the whole. It is not redundancy. It is diversity and depth.
Secure by design means that security is considered from the first moment of system conception, not
added as an afterthought. It is cheaper, more effective, and more sustainable than retrofitting.
Secure by default means that systems are configured securely out of the box: strong authentication,
minimal access, encrypted communication, and audit logging enabled. Users must deliberately weaken
security, not deliberately strengthen it.
Zero Trust, introduced architecturally in F3, is applied here as a security model: verify explicitly,
enforce least privilege, and continuously evaluate users, devices, and access requests.
Core model:
Confidentiality + Integrity + Availability = Foundation of Information Security
But modern security extends beyond CIA into identity, accountability, privacy, and resilience. The
executive who understands only CIA understands only the foundation.
Part II — Understand Threats, Vulnerabilities & Risk
F7.4 — Threats, Vulnerabilities & Attack Surface
Cyber risk materializes when threat meets vulnerability in a place the enterprise can be reached.
Threat is a potential cause of harm: a person, group, organisation, or event that could compromise
security. Threats are external, internal, accidental, or intentional.
Threat actor is the entity that poses the threat: nation-states, criminal organisations, hacktivists,

insiders, competitors, or opportunistic attackers. Different actors have different capabilities,
motivations, and targets.
Vulnerability is a weakness that could be exploited: unpatched software, misconfigured system, weak
password, missing control, or design flaw. Vulnerabilities exist in technology, processes, and people.
Exposure is the condition of being accessible to threat: internet-facing system, unprotected data,
privileged access, or supplier connection. Exposure does not create risk without threat and
vulnerability.
Attack vector is the path or method by which a threat actor exploits a vulnerability: phishing email,
compromised credential, unpatched server, malicious attachment, or social engineering call.
Attack surface is the total exposure of the enterprise: all the points where threat could meet
vulnerability. Attack surface grows with digital expansion, cloud adoption, remote work, and supplier
integration.
Exploit is the specific technique or tool used to take advantage of a vulnerability. Exploits are
developed, shared, sold, and automated.
Likelihood is the probability that a threat will exploit a vulnerability. It depends on threat capability,
vulnerability accessibility, control effectiveness, and target attractiveness.
128

Impact is the consequence if exploitation occurs: financial loss, operational disruption, reputational
damage, regulatory penalty, or competitive disadvantage.
Threat intelligence is the information about threats, actors, techniques, and campaigns that enables
proactive defense. It is not merely data. It is actionable insight.
Internal threats come from within the enterprise: employees, contractors, partners with legitimate
access. They may be malicious, negligent, or compromised.
External threats come from outside the enterprise: hackers, criminals, nation-states, competitors, and
activists. They may be targeted or opportunistic.
Insider threats are the deliberate or negligent actions of authorised users: data theft, sabotage, fraud,
or error. They are among the most difficult to detect because they exploit legitimate access.
Human error is the unintentional cause of security incidents: misconfiguration, misdelivery, weak
passwords, falling for phishing, or improper handling of data. Human error is not eliminated by
punishment. It is reduced by design, training, and culture.
Misconfiguration is the incorrect setup of systems, applications, or security controls: default
passwords, open ports, excessive permissions, disabled logging. Misconfiguration is one of the most
common and preventable vulnerabilities.
Legacy technology is outdated systems that are no longer supported, patched, or understood. Legacy
creates vulnerability because it cannot be secured against modern threats.
Supply-chain threats exploit the enterprise's suppliers, partners, and dependencies: compromised
software updates, trusted vendor access, or third-party data handling. Supply-chain attacks bypass
perimeter defenses by exploiting trust.

Cloud exposure is the risk arising from cloud misconfiguration, shared responsibility gaps, excessive
permissions, and inadequate monitoring. Cloud is not inherently insecure. But it is inherently different,
and different requires different discipline.
Social engineering manipulates people into breaking security procedures: pretexting, baiting, quid pro
quo, and phishing. It exploits human trust rather than technical weakness.
Phishing is the fraudulent attempt to obtain sensitive information by disguising as trustworthy: email,
message, call, or website. It is the most common initial attack vector.
Malware is malicious software: viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, and adware. It compromises systems,
steals data, or disrupts operations.
Ransomware is malware that encrypts data and demands payment for decryption. It has become one of
the most destructive and prevalent cyber threats.
Credential attacks steal or guess passwords, tokens, or keys: brute force, credential stuffing, password
spraying, and keylogging. Credentials are the keys to the kingdom.
Denial of service overwhelms systems with traffic or requests, rendering them unavailable. It disrupts
operations, damages reputation, and enables extortion.
At Foundation level, the emphasis is not on exploitation techniques. The executive needs to understand
what threats exist, what vulnerabilities and exposures enable them, and what business risk they create.
Core relationship:
129

Threat + Vulnerability + Exposure
Risk
→
With the important clarification that actual risk depends on likelihood, impact, and existing controls.
Threat, vulnerability, and exposure are necessary but not sufficient. Controls modify risk. Risk appetite
determines acceptability.
F7.5 — Technology & Cyber Risk Management
This is one of the major F7 sections. Read it carefully.
Risk management is the discipline that makes security rational. Without it, security becomes
superstition: more controls because more feels safer, more spending because spending signals concern,
more audits because audits demonstrate diligence. Risk management replaces superstition with
judgment.
Risk identification is the systematic discovery of what could harm the enterprise: assets, threats,
vulnerabilities, exposures, and scenarios. Identification requires imagination, evidence, and structured
techniques.
Risk analysis examines identified risks: likelihood, impact, controls, and dependencies. Analysis
enables prioritisation and treatment.
Risk assessment evaluates risks against criteria: risk appetite, risk tolerance, business impact, and
strategic importance. Assessment determines which risks demand action.
Likelihood is the probability that a risk will materialize. It is not precise. It is informed judgment based
on threat intelligence, historical data, vulnerability exposure, and control effectiveness.
Impact is the consequence if the risk materializes: financial, operational, reputational, regulatory, and
strategic. Impact must be assessed honestly, not minimized for comfort.
Inherent risk is the risk before controls: the raw exposure of assets to threats and vulnerabilities. It
answers: *"What is the risk if we do nothing?"*

Controls are the measures that reduce risk: preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, and
compensating. Controls modify likelihood, impact, or both.
Residual risk is the risk after controls: what remains despite protection. Residual risk is what the
enterprise actually lives with. It must be understood, accepted, and monitored.
Risk rating is the classification of risk by severity: critical, high, medium, low. Rating enables
prioritisation, communication, and governance.
Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk the enterprise is willing to pursue or retain in achieving its
objectives. It is established through governance and approved at the appropriate enterprise level. Risk
appetite is rarely zero because value creation inherently involves uncertainty.
Risk tolerance is the specific deviation from risk appetite that is acceptable in particular
circumstances. It provides operational flexibility within strategic boundaries.
Risk threshold is the point at which risk exceeds tolerance and triggers action: escalation, treatment, or
acceptance by higher authority.
Risk owner is the named individual accountable for a specific risk: understanding it, monitoring it,
treating it, and reporting it. Risk without owner is unmanaged risk.
130

Risk register is the inventory of identified risks: description, assessment, rating, owner, treatment,
status, and review date. It is the operational record of enterprise risk.
Risk treatment is the decision about what to do: avoid, mitigate, transfer, or accept.

Avoid — eliminate the risk by not engaging in the activity

Mitigate — reduce likelihood or impact through controls

Transfer / Share — shift consequence to another party through insurance, contract, or partnership

Accept — acknowledge the risk and prepare to respond if it materializes
Risk acceptance is the deliberate decision to live with residual risk. It requires understanding,
documentation, and appropriate authority. Unconscious acceptance is negligence.
Risk escalation raises risks that exceed tolerance, appetite, or authority to higher levels for decision.
Escalation must be fast, transparent, and decisive.
Risk monitoring tracks risk status, control effectiveness, threat evolution, and emerging exposure.
Monitoring enables early warning and proactive adjustment.
Emerging risk is the risk that has not yet materialized but may do so: new threats, new vulnerabilities,
new technologies, new regulations, or new business models. Emerging risk requires anticipation, not
merely reaction.
Core model:
Identify
Assess
Treat
Monitor
Report
→
→
→
→
This cycle is continuous. Risk management is not a phase. It is a permanent discipline.
Risk treatment:
Avoid
Mitigate
Transfer/Share
Accept
→
→
→
And the essential executive model:
Inherent Risk
Controls
Residual Risk
→
→
Inherent risk is what you start with. Controls are what you do about it. Residual risk is what you live
with. The discipline is in understanding all three and making deliberate choices.
F7.6 — Security Controls & Defense in Depth

Once risk is understood, it must be treated. Controls are the instruments of treatment.
Control types define what controls do:

Preventive — stop incidents before they occur: firewalls, access controls, encryption, authentication

Detective — identify incidents that have occurred: monitoring, logging, intrusion detection,
anomaly analysis

Corrective — restore systems after incidents: backup, recovery, patching, remediation

Deterrent — discourage attackers: warnings, penalties, visible security, prosecution

Compensating — provide alternative protection when primary controls fail or are impractical:
manual verification, additional monitoring, or redundant processes

Recovery controls — ensure restoration of operations after disruption: failover, redundancy,
business continuity, disaster recovery
Control nature defines how controls are implemented:
131


Administrative — policies, procedures, training, and governance

Technical — software, hardware, and automated mechanisms

Physical — locks, guards, access cards, and environmental controls
Defense in depth is the layered approach: multiple controls at multiple levels so that no single failure
compromises security. The layers are:
People
Process
Identity
Endpoint
Network
Application
Data
Infrastructure
→
→
→
→
→
→
→
→
Monitoring
Each layer provides protection. Each layer backs up the others. The attacker who breaches one layer
encounters another.
Control objectives define what each control must achieve: prevent unauthorized access, detect
anomalous behaviour, ensure data integrity, maintain service availability. Objectives must be specific
and measurable.
Control effectiveness measures whether controls achieve their objectives: testing, audit, metrics, and
incident analysis. Ineffective controls are worse than no controls because they create false confidence.
Control ownership is the accountability for control design, implementation, maintenance, and
effectiveness. Every control must have a named owner.
Control testing verifies that controls work as intended through automated testing, manual review,
assurance activities, penetration testing, or exercises as appropriate. The frequency should be
proportionate to risk and control criticality.
Control gaps are the deficiencies where controls are missing, ineffective, or bypassed. Gaps must be
identified, assessed, and treated.
Compensating controls provide alternative protection when primary controls cannot be implemented:
additional monitoring, manual verification, or process redundancy. Compensating controls must be
proportionate and effective.

Continuous control monitoring uses automated checks, metrics, and exception reporting to provide
more timely assurance. It complements rather than replaces independent or periodic audit.
Key principle:
No single security control is sufficient.
The enterprise that relies on one control — one firewall, one password policy, one backup system — has
one point of failure. Defense in depth ensures that security survives failure.
Part III — Protect Identity, Infrastructure, Applications & Data
F7.7 — Identity & Access Management
Identity has become the primary security boundary. The perimeter is no longer the network edge. It is
the individual user, device, and service.
Digital identity is the representation of a user, device, or service in the enterprise's systems: who they
are, what they can access, and what they have done.
Authentication verifies identity: passwords, tokens, biometrics, certificates, or behavioural signals.
Authentication must be strong, appropriate to risk, and resistant to compromise.
132

Authorization determines what an authenticated identity can do: read, write, delete, approve, or
administer. Authorization must be granular, appropriate, and continuously verified.
Identification is the initial claim of identity: username, email, device ID, or service principal.
Identification must be unique, verifiable, and protected.
MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) requires multiple proofs of identity: something you know,
something you have, something you are. MFA is one of the most effective controls against credential
compromise.
SSO (Single Sign-On) enables users to authenticate once and access multiple services. SSO improves
user experience and security consistency but creates concentration risk if the identity provider fails or
is compromised.
Federation extends identity across organisational boundaries: partners, suppliers, and customers
accessing shared resources with their own credentials. Federation requires trust, standards, and
governance.
Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) grants permissions based on job role: managers have these rights,
analysts have those. RBAC simplifies administration but can become coarse and outdated.
Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) grants permissions based on multiple attributes: user role,
location, device, time, and data sensitivity. ABAC is more granular and dynamic but more complex to
implement.
Least privilege means that access is granted at the minimum level necessary for the specific task, for
the minimum time required. It is not a one-time decision. It is a continuous discipline.
Privileged Access Management (PAM) governs the powerful accounts that control systems, data, and
infrastructure: admin accounts, service accounts, root accounts, and emergency access. Privileged

access is the most dangerous and must be the most controlled.
Privileged accounts are the keys to the kingdom. Their compromise is catastrophic. They must be
minimal, monitored, time-limited, and heavily audited.
Joiner–Mover–Leaver is the lifecycle discipline: provisioning access when someone joins, adjusting
access when they move roles, and revoking access when they leave. Failure at any point creates orphan
accounts, excessive permissions, and invisible risk.
Access provisioning grants access based on role, request, or workflow. It must be governed,
documented, and verified.
Access reviews periodically verify that existing access remains appropriate: managers confirm their
team's rights, owners validate their resources' permissions, and auditors sample for compliance.
Segregation of duties divides critical functions among multiple people to prevent fraud, error, and
abuse. No single person should control an entire sensitive process.
Service accounts are the non-human identities that applications and systems use to interact. They are
often invisible, poorly managed, and dangerously powerful. Service account governance is essential.
Machine identities are the digital credentials of devices, services, APIs, and IoT endpoints. They
outnumber human identities and are often less managed.
Passwordless authentication replaces passwords with stronger factors: biometrics, hardware tokens,
or cryptographic keys. It reduces credential risk but requires infrastructure and cultural adaptation.
133

Identity governance is the comprehensive discipline of managing identities throughout their lifecycle:
creation, modification, review, and termination. It ensures that the right people have the right access
for the right reasons at the right times.
Zero Trust relationship means that identity verification is continuous, not one-time. Every access
request is evaluated based on identity, device, behaviour, and context. Trust is never assumed.
Core model:
Identify
Authenticate
Authorize
Monitor
Review
Revoke
→
→
→
→
→
Identity is established. Authentication verifies. Authorization permits. Monitoring observes. Review
validates. Revoke terminates. Each step is essential.
Important principle:
Access should be granted based on business need, limited to what is required, monitored while
active, and removed when no longer justified.
F7.8 — Infrastructure, Network, Endpoint & Cloud Security
The technical protection domains must work together as a coherent system. Isolated excellence creates
systemic weakness.
Network security protects connectivity: segmentation, firewalls, intrusion detection, intrusion
prevention, and secure remote access.
Segmentation divides the network into zones, limiting lateral movement. It contains breaches and
reduces blast radius.
Firewalls control traffic between zones based on rules: permit, deny, inspect. They are necessary but
not sufficient.
IDS/IPS (Intrusion Detection/Prevention Systems) monitor traffic for malicious patterns and either
alert or block. They detect known threats but may miss novel attacks.
Secure remote access enables authorised users to connect from outside the enterprise: VPN, Zero Trust
Network Access, or privileged access workstations. Remote access has expanded dramatically and must
be correspondingly controlled.

VPN (Virtual Private Network) encrypts traffic between remote users and enterprise networks. It
provides secure connectivity but does not verify user trustworthiness.
NAC (Network Access Control) restricts network access based on device identity, health, and
compliance. Untrusted or unhealthy devices are quarantined.
Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) provides application-level, context-aware access based on identity,
device, policy, and risk. It can complement or replace traditional VPN access in appropriate use cases.
DNS security protects the domain name system from hijacking, poisoning, and exfiltration. DNS is often
overlooked but critically important.
Endpoint security protects devices: endpoint protection platforms, endpoint detection and response,
hardening, patch management, and device management.
Endpoint protection prevents malware and unauthorized activity: antivirus, anti-malware, application
control, and device control.
134

EDR/XDR (Endpoint Detection and Response / Extended Detection and Response) monitors
endpoints for suspicious behaviour, detects threats, and enables rapid response. EDR is endpoint-
focused. XDR extends across networks, cloud, and applications.
Hardening reduces attack surface by disabling unnecessary services, removing default accounts,
enforcing strong configurations, and minimizing exposure.
Patch management applies security updates promptly and consistently. Unpatched vulnerabilities are
among the most exploited attack vectors.
Device management governs the configuration, security, and compliance of endpoints: mobile device
management, unified endpoint management, and bring-your-own-device policies.
Encryption protects data at rest and in transit: full disk encryption, file encryption, database
encryption, and communication encryption. Encryption is essential but must be accompanied by key
management.
Infrastructure security protects the foundational systems: secure configuration, vulnerability
management, patch management, hardening, and administrative access control.
Secure configuration ensures that systems are deployed with security-enabled settings: not defaults,
not convenience, but protection.
Vulnerability management identifies, assesses, prioritizes, and remediates security weaknesses:
scanning, assessment, patching, and verification.
Administrative access controls the powerful accounts that manage infrastructure. Administrative
access must be minimal, monitored, time-limited, and heavily audited.
Cloud security addresses the unique risks of cloud environments: shared responsibility, configuration,
identity, encryption, and monitoring.
Shared responsibility model defines what the cloud provider secures and what the enterprise secures.

Misunderstanding this model is a leading cause of cloud security failure.
Cloud configuration ensures that cloud resources are deployed securely: not default settings, not
excessive permissions, not open storage, not unencrypted data.
IAM (Identity and Access Management) in cloud governs who can access cloud resources, what they
can do, and how their access is monitored and reviewed.
Encryption in cloud protects data at rest and in transit, and in some architectures can also protect data
during processing. Key ownership may be provider-managed, customer-managed, or supported by
hardware security modules.
Cloud monitoring tracks cloud security events, configuration changes, access patterns, and compliance
status. Cloud visibility is essential.
CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Management) conceptually ensures that cloud configurations remain
secure over time: continuous assessment, drift detection, and remediation guidance.
SaaS security governs the enterprise's use of software-as-a-service: access control, data protection,
configuration, integration security, and vendor assessment.
Hybrid environments combine on-premises and cloud infrastructure. They require consistent security
across boundaries: identity, policy, monitoring, and response.
135

Key principle:
Security architecture should assume that prevention can fail and design for containment,
detection, and recovery.
No perimeter is perfect. No control is absolute. The discipline is in layering defenses so that breach does
not become catastrophe.
F7.9 — Application, API & DevSecOps Security
Applications are where business value meets technical vulnerability. Their security must be built in, not
bolted on.
Application security protects software from design through operation: requirements, design, coding,
testing, deployment, and maintenance.
Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC) embeds security into every phase of development:
security requirements, threat modeling, secure coding, security testing, and secure deployment.
Secure coding practices prevent common vulnerabilities: input validation, output encoding,
authentication, authorization, session management, and error handling. Developers must be trained,
tools must support, and governance must enforce.
Security requirements define what the application must protect, against what threats, with what
controls, and to what standard. Requirements must be specific, testable, and traced.
Threat modeling systematically identifies threats to an application: what could go wrong, where, how,
and with what impact. It is design-stage risk assessment.
Code review examines source code for security flaws: manual review, automated scanning, and peer
inspection. Review catches what tools miss and tools catch what reviewers overlook.
SAST (Static Application Security Testing) analyzes source code for vulnerabilities without executing
it. It finds coding flaws early but may miss runtime issues.
DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) tests running applications for vulnerabilities. It finds

runtime issues but may miss design flaws.
Software Composition Analysis identifies third-party and open-source components, their versions,
and their known vulnerabilities. Modern applications are mostly assembled, not written. Component
security is application security.
Vulnerability testing systematically identifies security weaknesses: automated scanning, manual
testing, and configuration review.
Penetration testing simulates attack to identify exploitable vulnerabilities. It validates security but
provides only a point-in-time assessment.
API security protects the interfaces that connect applications: authentication, authorization, input
validation, rate limiting, encryption, and monitoring. APIs are the new perimeter.
Authentication/authorization for APIs ensures that only legitimate consumers access appropriate
functions with proper permissions.
Secrets management protects the credentials, tokens, and keys that applications use to authenticate:
vaults, rotation, and least privilege.
136

CI/CD security protects the pipeline that builds, tests, and deploys software: code integrity, access
control, artifact verification, and deployment approval.
DevSecOps integrates security into DevOps: automated security testing, vulnerability scanning,
compliance checks, and threat modeling as part of every build and deployment. It is security by design,
operationalized.
Dependency risk is the vulnerability introduced by third-party components: libraries, frameworks, and
services. Dependency management is essential application security.
Open-source risk is the vulnerability in freely available software components: known vulnerabilities,
unmaintained projects, license obligations, and supply-chain exposure.
Software supply chain is the sequence of components, tools, and processes that produce software:
code, dependencies, build tools, repositories, and distribution. Supply-chain security ensures integrity at
every step.
Security testing before production reduces the likelihood that significant vulnerabilities reach live
environments through practices such as SAST, DAST, dependency scanning, configuration review, and
risk-based penetration testing. Security validation should also continue after deployment.
Core progression:
Design Securely
Build Securely
Test Securely
Deploy Securely
Operate Securely
→
→
→
→
Security at each stage enables security at the next. Security failure at any stage compromises all that
follow.
F7.10 — Data Protection, Privacy & Information Governance
Data is the enterprise's most valuable asset and its most vulnerable exposure. Protecting it requires
discipline across the full lifecycle.
Data classification categorizes data by sensitivity and criticality: public, internal, confidential,

restricted. Classification determines protection requirements, access controls, and handling procedures.
Data ownership is the business accountability for data definition, quality, access policy, and
appropriate use. Data owners are business leaders, not IT administrators.
Data sensitivity reflects the harm that unauthorized disclosure, modification, or destruction would
cause: personal information, financial data, intellectual property, strategic plans, and operational
secrets.
Data lifecycle is the journey from creation to destruction: capture, store, process, transmit, archive, and
dispose. Security must be maintained at every stage.
Data minimization collects and retains only what is necessary. Excess data increases risk, cost, and
compliance burden without creating value.
Access control restricts data access to authorised users, for authorised purposes, under authorised
conditions. Access must be granted, monitored, reviewed, and revoked.
Encryption at rest protects stored data: databases, files, backups, and archives. Encryption ensures that
stolen data remains unreadable without keys.
Encryption in transit protects data moving across networks: VPN, TLS, and secure protocols.
Encryption prevents interception and eavesdropping.
137

Key management governs the creation, storage, distribution, rotation, and destruction of encryption
keys. Keys are the guardians of encrypted data. Compromised keys destroy encryption's value.
DLP (Data Loss Prevention) monitors, detects, and prevents unauthorized data movement:
exfiltration, misdelivery, and improper access. DLP is not perfect but raises the bar for data theft.
Data masking replaces sensitive data with fictional but realistic values for testing, development, and
analysis. Masking enables utility without exposure.
Tokenization replaces sensitive data with non-sensitive tokens that reference the original data stored
securely elsewhere. Tokenization reduces exposure in operational systems.
Backup protects data against loss, corruption, and destruction. Backup must be regular, verified,
encrypted, and tested.
Retention defines how long data is kept: regulatory requirements, business need, and risk
management. Excessive retention increases risk and cost.
Secure disposal ensures that data is irrecoverably destroyed when no longer needed: shredding,
degaussing, cryptographic erasure, and certified destruction.
Data sovereignty is the legal jurisdiction where data is stored and governed. Sovereignty determines
applicable law, regulatory requirements, and government access.
Data residency is the physical location where data is stored. Residency affects latency, sovereignty,
compliance, and cost.
Privacy is the protection of personal information: collection, use, sharing, retention, and rights of
individuals. Privacy is not merely compliance. It is ethical obligation and business trust.
Personal data is any information relating to an identified or identifiable individual. Its protection is
legally mandated, ethically required, and commercially essential.

Privacy by design embeds privacy into systems and processes from conception: data minimization,
purpose limitation, transparency, and user control.
Consent at a conceptual level means that individuals understand and agree to how their data is used.
Consent must be informed, voluntary, specific, and revocable.
Regulatory obligations for data protection vary by jurisdiction: GDPR, CCPA, PIPEDA, PDPL, and
others. Compliance is necessary but not sufficient for genuine protection.
Important distinction:
Cybersecurity protects systems. Data protection protects information. Privacy protects people's
rights and appropriate use of personal information.
These three are related but distinct. Confusing them creates gaps: systems secured while data is
exposed, data encrypted while privacy is violated.
Avoid turning F7 into a privacy-law manual. The executive must understand privacy principles,
obligations, and implications. Detailed legal compliance belongs to specialists.
138

Part IV — Detect, Respond & Recover
F7.11 — Security Monitoring & Security Operations
Detection is the moment when prevention fails and response begins. Without detection, breaches
persist, damage compounds, and recovery becomes impossible.
Security Operations Center (SOC) is the centralised function that monitors, detects, analyzes, and
responds to security threats and incidents. It is the operational heart of cybersecurity.
SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) collects, correlates, and analyzes security logs
and events from across the enterprise. It provides visibility, detection, and investigation capability.
Security logs are the records of security-relevant activity: authentication attempts, access events,
configuration changes, and system alerts. Logs are the forensic evidence of security.
Security events are observable occurrences with potential security relevance: failed logins, policy
violations, configuration drift, or anomalous behaviour.
Alerts are the notifications that something requires security attention: threshold exceeded, pattern
matched, or anomaly detected. Alerts must be actionable, accurate, and prioritised.
Use cases are the defined scenarios that detection systems monitor: brute force attack, lateral
movement, data exfiltration, privilege escalation. Use cases translate threat intelligence into detection
capability.
Detection rules are the specific logic that identifies suspicious activity: signatures, thresholds,
behavioural patterns, and statistical anomalies.
Threat intelligence feeds detection with information about threats, actors, techniques, and indicators.
Intelligence enables proactive and contextual detection.
Indicators of Compromise (IoCs) are the observable artifacts of intrusion: IP addresses, file hashes,

domain names, and registry keys. IoCs enable rapid identification of known threats.
Behavioural analytics detects anomalies by comparing current activity to baseline behaviour: unusual
login times, atypical data access, or abnormal network traffic.
EDR/XDR provides endpoint visibility, threat detection, and response capability. EDR is endpoint-
focused. XDR extends across networks, cloud, email, and applications.
SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) automates security operations: alert
triage, incident enrichment, containment actions, and response workflows. SOAR accelerates response
but requires mature processes.
Security monitoring is the continuous observation of security-relevant activity: network traffic, system
behaviour, user actions, and configuration state.
Detection engineering conceptually develops, tests, and maintains the logic that identifies threats. It is
the craft of turning threat knowledge into operational detection.
False positives are alerts on benign activity. They consume analyst time, erode confidence, and create
alert fatigue.
Alert fatigue occurs when analysts receive too many alerts, too few of which are actionable. It leads to
ignored alerts, delayed response, and missed incidents.
139

Escalation raises security events to incident response when they exceed defined thresholds: severity,
impact, or uncertainty.
Security dashboards provide real-time visibility into security posture: threats detected, incidents open,
vulnerabilities remediated, and controls effective.
Core model:
Collect
Correlate
Detect
Investigate
Respond
→
→
→
→
Data is collected from across the enterprise. Events are correlated into meaningful patterns. Threats are
detected through rules and analytics. Suspected incidents are investigated. Confirmed incidents are
responded to.
Boundary:
F6 monitors service health. F7 monitors security threats and suspicious behaviour.
Both require visibility. Both generate alerts. Both demand response. But their purpose, tools, and
disciplines differ.
F7.12 — Cybersecurity Incident Response
Governance determines escalation thresholds, communication protocols, decision authority, evidence
requirements, and regulatory or stakeholder notification obligations during an incident.
This is another major section. Read it carefully.
Security incidents are not operational incidents. They require distinct discipline, distinct governance,
and distinct expertise.
Security event vs. security incident distinguishes an observable occurrence from an event or series of
events that meets the organisation’s incident criteria and requires coordinated response. Events are
monitored and triaged; incidents trigger formal response.
Incident classification categorizes incidents by type: malware, phishing, data breach, insider threat,
denial of service, or supply-chain compromise. Classification determines response procedures.
Severity ranks incidents by impact and urgency: critical, high, medium, low. Severity determines
resource allocation, escalation, and communication.

Detection is the identification of a potential security incident: monitoring alert, user report, threat
intelligence, or automated detection.
Analysis investigates the incident: scope, impact, method, attribution, and timeline. Analysis must be
rapid but thorough.
Containment limits the incident's spread: isolate affected systems, revoke compromised credentials,
block malicious traffic, and preserve evidence. Containment must be swift to prevent escalation.
Eradication removes the threat: delete malware, close vulnerabilities, eliminate backdoors, and restore
integrity. Eradication must be complete to prevent recurrence.
Recovery restores normal operations: rebuild systems, restore data from clean backups, re-enable
services, and verify integrity. Recovery must be deliberate to avoid re-infection.
Evidence preservation maintains the integrity of incident artifacts: logs, files, memory dumps, and
network captures. Evidence may be required for investigation, prosecution, or regulatory reporting.
140

Forensics conceptually examines digital evidence to understand what happened, how, when, and by
whom. Forensics requires expertise, tools, and legal awareness.
Communication during security incidents is critical: internal coordination, executive briefing, user
notification, customer communication, regulatory reporting, and media response. Communication must
be accurate, timely, and controlled.
Executive escalation engages senior leadership when incidents exceed defined thresholds: business
impact, regulatory exposure, public visibility, or strategic risk. Executives must be informed, not
surprised.
Legal involvement addresses regulatory obligations, contractual requirements, liability, and evidence
preservation. Legal must be engaged early, not after decisions are made.
Regulatory notification may be required for data breaches, security failures, or compliance incidents.
Notification requirements vary by jurisdiction, industry, and breach severity. Timing, content, and
recipient are legally defined.
Vendor involvement engages suppliers whose products, services, or access are implicated. Vendor
relationships must include incident coordination protocols.
Crisis coordination manages incidents that threaten enterprise operations, reputation, or survival.
Crisis coordination requires executive leadership, cross-functional response, and external
communication.
Post-incident review examines what happened, how it was handled, what worked, what failed, and
what must improve. It is not blame. It is organisational learning.
Lessons learned capture insights from incidents: detection gaps, response failures, control weaknesses,
and process improvements. They must be documented, shared, and applied.
Core lifecycle:
Prepare
Detect
Analyse
Contain
Eradicate
Recover
Learn
→
→
→
→
→
→

Preparation enables effective response. Detection triggers action. Analysis informs decisions.
Containment limits damage. Eradication removes threat. Recovery restores operations. Learning
prevents recurrence.
Important distinction:
Operational incident management restores service. Cyber incident response must restore service
while also containing the threat, preserving evidence, and preventing further compromise.
The rush to restore can destroy evidence, re-enable attackers, and compound damage. The discipline is
in balancing speed of recovery with thoroughness of response.
Part V — Resilience & Continuity
F7.13 — Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery
Governance sets the risk appetite that informs recovery objectives, resilience investment, continuity
priorities, and executive acceptance of residual exposure.
Disruption is inevitable. The leadership question is whether critical business outcomes can continue
and whether technology can be recovered within agreed priorities.
141

Business Continuity is the discipline of maintaining critical business activities at an acceptable level
during and after disruption. It is broader than technology recovery and includes people, facilities,
suppliers, communications, information, and alternative ways of working.
Critical business processes and services are the activities and services whose disruption would create
unacceptable financial, operational, regulatory, reputational, safety, or customer impact. Continuity
planning begins by identifying what is truly critical and why.
Business Impact Analysis (BIA) evaluates how disruption affects critical activities over time. It
establishes priorities, dependencies, impact tolerances, and the information needed to design continuity
and recovery strategies.
Maximum tolerable disruption is the point beyond which disruption creates unacceptable
consequences. Organisations may use different terminology, but the leadership purpose is the same:
understand how long critical activities can be impaired before the impact becomes intolerable.
Continuity strategies define how critical activities will continue when normal arrangements are
unavailable: alternate locations, remote work, manual procedures, alternative suppliers, redundant
capacity, or controlled degraded service.
Disaster Recovery (DR) is the technology-focused discipline of restoring systems, infrastructure,
applications, data, and supporting technology services following significant disruption. DR supports
business continuity; it does not replace it.
Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the target time within which a service or technology capability
should be restored after disruption.
Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the maximum targeted amount of data loss measured in time. It

determines how much data the organisation is prepared to recreate or lose following recovery.
Backup provides recoverable copies of data and configurations. Effective backup requires appropriate
frequency, protection, isolation where needed, integrity verification, retention, and restoration testing.
Replication and failover can reduce recovery time by maintaining alternate copies or environments.
They improve resilience but can also replicate corruption or compromise, so they must be designed and
tested carefully.
Recovery environments may include alternate data centers, cloud recovery, secondary regions, warm
or hot standby arrangements, or rebuilt infrastructure. The correct strategy depends on business
criticality, cost, architecture, risk, and recovery objectives.
DR plans define responsibilities, activation criteria, recovery sequence, dependencies, communication,
technical procedures, validation, and return-to-normal arrangements.
Testing and exercising confirm whether continuity and recovery arrangements work under realistic
conditions. Tabletop exercises test decisions and coordination; technical recovery tests validate
restoration; broader simulations test end-to-end resilience.

F7.14 — Operational & Cyber Resilience
Resilience is broader than availability, continuity, or disaster recovery. It is the enterprise's ability to
anticipate disruption, withstand impact, continue critical outcomes, recover effectively, adapt, and
learn.
Operational resilience focuses on maintaining important business services within acceptable impact
tolerances when disruption occurs. It considers technology, people, processes, facilities, suppliers, data,
and other dependencies as one operating system.
Cyber resilience applies the same principle to cyber disruption: the ability to prepare for attacks,
withstand compromise, contain damage, recover trusted operations, and adapt controls based on what
was learned.
Resilience vs. availability is the distinction between normal service reliability and performance under
disruption. High availability reduces interruption; resilience assumes interruption can still occur and
prepares the enterprise to absorb it.
Resilience vs. continuity is the distinction between a broader organisational capability and the specific
plans used to continue critical activities. Continuity is a major component of resilience, not the whole of
it.
Critical services and dependencies must be understood end to end. A resilient application can still fail
as a business service if identity, network, data, supplier, facility, or people dependencies are
unavailable.
Redundancy provides alternate components or capacity. Diversity reduces the risk that identical
components fail for the same reason. Fault tolerance allows systems to continue operating despite
component failure.

Graceful degradation allows a service to continue at reduced functionality rather than fail completely.
For critical services, reduced but controlled operation may be more valuable than total outage.
Scenario planning asks what happens when expected controls fail: identity provider unavailable, cloud
region disrupted, ransomware spreads, supplier access is compromised, or key personnel are
unavailable.
Stress testing and exercises expose weaknesses before real disruption does. They should test not only
technology recovery but decisions, communications, suppliers, manual workarounds, data integrity,
and executive coordination.
Adaptive capacity is the ability to change plans, controls, architecture, and operating practices as
threats and business conditions evolve.
Key principle:
Resilience is not the ability to prevent every failure. It is the ability to continue, recover, adapt,
and learn when failure occurs.
